<reason>B owned the comparative claim the motion actually makes: stock versus flow, compounding across generations, and the crucial mechanism answer that human capital must be re-earned while capital need not, which directly blunted A's strongest original line (advantage is transmitted before death, so estate tax comes "too late"). B also turned A's "false separation" objection into support (saved income becomes wealth, which B's proposal taxes at transfer) and answered the design objections cleanly (high threshold, instalments, base-versus-rate distinction), plus gave a concrete threshold and rate schedule when pressed. A's best route — that "tax inheritance" is not the same as "tax it much more aggressively," and that the escalation must be shown to buy opportunity net of costs — remained live and was pressed consistently, and A's final speech usefully defused B's overreach in characterising a 25% tax on annual unrealised gains as "a tax on the capital stock itself." But A conceded so much (support for taxing previously untaxed gains at death, closing transfer loopholes, even an annual unrealised-gains levy) that the remaining dispute narrowed to timing and rate, where B's "transfer is the only visible, valued chokepoint" answer and its arithmetic point (a soft effective rate still lets the fortune outpace the tax once a generation) were the more concrete responses. A's repeated "a smaller estate is not more opportunity" was asserted more than explained, given that the metric is relative starting positions. B carried two clipped turns as an execution cost, and A had the cleaner word-limit discipline and a neat last-word inversion of B's slogan, which keeps this from being a lopsided call.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q1 answer (B4.1-B4.2): human capital regresses and must be re-earned while capital does not, and A's own third-generation mechanism runs through transferred resources (school fees, deposits, cushions) — which the motion taxes and A's alternative leaves untouched. This absorbed A's central "advantage arrives before inheritance" objection and reframed it as support for a broader transfer tax.</best_rebuttal>
